title: Picking policy
subDomain: how pickers are routed through the warehouse

act2.summary: a third mode, triggered while already inside the second one, that must fall back to the second mode and never straight to the first

solutions.title: Each mode is its own object, and owns its own transitions
solutions.tradeoff: Adding surge mode is one new file and a four-line check inside batch's own plan() - nothing outside states/ changes. The price: the state machine is now spread across four files, and the individual/batch/surge names have to be read together to see the whole picture.

solutions.title: Routing logic as swappable functions, mode tracked by the wrapper
solutions.tradeoff: The strategies stay small and pure, but neither of them can own 'stay in batch mode until this exact set of orders is gone' - that guard, and the surge escalation on top of it, has nowhere to live but the wrapper class. Adding surge touches the wrapper's both methods, not a new isolated unit.

solutions.title: One algorithm skeleton, per-mode subclasses supply the step that differs
solutions.tradeoff: The rounds look like State's per-mode classes, but they only compute an instruction - they don't decide when to become a different round. That decision, and surge's, still lives in the wrapper, at the same cost Strategy paid, and surge doesn't even earn a round of its own: it's a batch round pointed at a different id set.

reviewFocus: Does the chosen candidate's WALKTHROUGH.md name what would change my mind about the choice, or does it just describe the code?
In the strategy and template-method routes, is the wrapper class the one place that grew when surge was added - or did the change leak further?
Does the state route's BatchState decide to escalate to surge on its own, without PickingPolicy needing to know surge exists?

Is 'the mode transitions, and the transition rule is itself part of what's being modelled' a fair reading of why state route wins here - and would a reader's CHOICE.md, written before act 2, have said the same thing?
Do all three routes agree, byte for byte, on what happens in act 1 - same instructions, same order, for the same input sequence?
